name: Vera Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you start by telling me a bit about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Vera, I'm 27, and I'm the education and community reporter at the Evening Star, the paper for our cathedral city and the towns around it. I cover schools, church news, charities and the odd planning row. I'm single, I rent a flat two streets from my parents, and I sing in the choir at St Anne's on Sundays.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Walk me through a normal working day. What do you do, what do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My mornings are school governors' papers, council agendas and phone calls to head teachers, who mostly don't want to talk to me. Afternoons I'm out at a school play or a food bank or a fundraising walk. I like stories where ordinary people do something good and nobody notices. What wears me out is that I'm still not quick, and my editor, Helen, often turns my first paragraph inside out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm glad, because I like the paper the way it is. At work I'd say we can stop worrying and get back to reporting. I'd say it at church coffee too, when people ask if the paper's closing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm not safe just because AI stalls. The Star went from printing daily to three days a week last year, and they didn't replace two people who left. I live on one wage, so if my job went, there's nobody else's pay to fall back on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the AI tool now and then to pull the main points out of long council papers, because a colleague showed me and it works. I'd ask Helen for feedback on my intros each week. And I'd keep saving, aiming for five months instead of three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly relieved, with a worry in the back of my mind. A world where AI fizzles out still has an evening paper that only prints three days a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you live on one wage. What would happen if it stopped?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have about three months, and then I'd be asking my parents for help, which I'd hate. They'd say yes straight away. That's how my family works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the Star would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Helen, a bit, because she does three people's jobs now. And Martin on the sports desk, who's 59 and can't move to another city. He'd struggle more than me.

say: I'd say I'm **glad** and want to get back to reporting.
I'd tell people at **church coffee** the paper isn't closing yet.
think: I think the Star printing **three days a week** shows the risk is already here.
I live on **one wage**, with nobody else's pay to fall back on.
do: Use the **AI tool** now and then for long council papers.
Ask Helen for **weekly feedback** on my intros.
Raise savings from three to **five months**.
feel: Mostly **relieved**, with a **worry** in the background.
S0.quote: A world where AI fizzles out still has an evening paper that only prints three days a week.
fieldNote: Vera's pressure is the Star's **shrinking print run**, which predates AI.
Living on **one wage** makes her more exposed than she lets on.
Her **family** is her real safety net, and she's proud of how they help.

steps.text: Use the AI tool to summarise long council papers
Ask Helen for weekly feedback on story intros
Raise savings from three to five months of costs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say businesses have a right to use new tools, but the paper should keep a person at the school gate and the church door. I'd say people need to step up and learn, not wait to be rescued. I'd say it kindly, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, a lot of my mornings would go to the software: summarising council papers, writing up press releases from schools and charities. That's writing and checking, right at the top of the card. If the Star cut another reporter, a junior on one beat would be easy to lose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the tools properly once I'd seen them work for Helen, so I could cover more ground. I'd save harder, skipping my summer trip to the coast. And I'd look at what I could do with my degree that's face to face, maybe teaching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but determined. I'd feel like I had to earn my place again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people need to step up. Does that apply to you too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, it does, and that's what makes it uncomfortable. I've always said people should learn new skills instead of waiting for help, and now I'm the one who has to learn them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why teaching?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum was a school secretary for twenty years, and I've spent three years watching good teachers on my beat. It's work with people, in a room. And schools are in every town.

say: I'd say businesses can use **new tools**, but keep a person at the school gate.
I'd say people should **step up and learn**, kindly put.
think: I think my **mornings of summaries** and press releases would go to software.
A **junior on one beat** would be easy for the Star to lose.
do: Learn the AI tools once **Helen** uses them.
Skip the **summer trip** to the coast and save harder.
Look into **teaching** as a face-to-face job.
S1.quote: I've always said people should learn new skills instead of waiting for help, and now I'm the one who has to learn them.
fieldNote: Vera applies her own **self-reliance** belief to herself, and finds it uncomfortable.
She'd adopt AI once **proven** by her editor, in line with her steady nature.
Teaching appeals because of her **mum's** school work and her beat.

steps.text: Learn the newsroom AI tools after Helen starts using them
Skip the summer coast trip and save the money
Look at teaching jobs and training routes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say families and churches need to look after each other, because this is too fast for anyone else. I'd say the government should back apprenticeships, not just pay benefits. I'd keep it calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my job's gone within a year. Almost all of it is thinking work, so I don't get the three extra years. Teaching would change fast too, at least the marking and planning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my brother Tom, who's a plumber, whether he'd take me on as an apprentice, because hands-on work lasts till about 2031. I'd give up my flat and move back to my parents to save the rent. And I'd stop spending on anything but the basics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, really. And a bit humbled, going home at 28.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Plumbing is a big change. Do you think you'd stick at it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have to. I'd rather crawl under a sink as my brother's apprentice than sit at home waiting for a newsroom that doesn't exist any more. Tom would tease me for a month, then teach me properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And when the robots come for plumbing around 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I honestly don't know. Old houses with odd pipes might take longer. I'd be praying a lot, and saving every penny.

say: I'd say **families and churches** need to look after each other.
I'd say government should back **apprenticeships**, not just benefits.
think: I think my job's **gone within a year**.
Almost all my work is **thinking work**, so the robot gap doesn't help me.
do: Ask my brother Tom for a **plumbing apprenticeship**.
Give up my flat and **move back** to my parents.
S2.quote: I'd rather crawl under a sink as my brother's apprentice than sit at home waiting for a newsroom that doesn't exist any more.
fieldNote: Vera turns to a **hands-on trade** through family, using the robot gap.
Her traditional values show in favouring **apprenticeships** over benefits.
She doesn't know what happens **after 2031** and says so.

steps.text: Start a plumbing apprenticeship with her brother Tom
Give up the flat and move back to her parents
Rely on her parents for housing and help

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time to plan, so families and firms should plan. I'd write about schools getting ready. I'd keep it practical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd use the time to get into teaching. I'd be 32 by 2031, with some years of classroom work behind me. Even if AI does the marking, someone has to be in the room with thirty children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd use the AI tools at the Star to stay useful and save hard. In year two I'd start a one-year teacher training course, probably for primary. And I'd stay in my flat for now, close to my parents.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I'd feel like I had a plan. That helps a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you pay for teacher training on one wage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's usually a grant for training, and I'd have savings by then. I'd move back home for that one year if I had to. My parents have already offered, before I've even asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you miss about the paper?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The good-news stories. The food bank volunteers, the choir that raises money for the hospice. Nobody pays a reporter to cover a church choir raising money for the hospice, but I'd miss those stories most.

say: I'd say five years is **time to plan**, so families and firms should plan.
I'd write practical stories about **schools getting ready**.
think: I think I'd get into **teaching** before 2031.
Someone still has to be **in the room** with thirty children.
do: Use **AI tools** at the Star and save hard this year.
Start a one-year **teacher training** course in year two.
Stay in my flat **near my parents** for now.
S3.quote: Nobody pays a reporter to cover a church choir raising money for the hospice, but I'd miss those stories most.
fieldNote: Five years lets Vera take the **teaching route** she named in the mild scenario.
She leans on **family** offers before even asking.
Her love of **good-news stories** is what she'd mourn.

steps.text: Use the Star's AI tools to cover more stories
Save hard toward a year of teacher training
Start a one-year primary teacher training course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so there's no need to panic. People should get on with their lives and plan sensibly. I'd say that at church and at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd stay at the Star and try to become good at the job. I'd like to have a family by then, and I'd want my work settled. Ten years gives me room to think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the tools where they help and keep improving my writing. I'd save steadily. In five years or so I'd look again at teaching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm. The paper's still a worry, but not a big one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned a family. Would this picture change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I'd still want children one day, and a computer taking newsroom jobs in ten years isn't a reason to put that off. That's in God's hands more than mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would change your mind and make you move sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the Star dropped to one print day, or Helen left. Either would tell me the end was nearer than ten years.

say: I'd say ten years is **plenty**, so no need to panic.
I'd tell people to **plan sensibly** and get on with life.
think: I think I'd stay at the Star and get **good at the job**.
Ten years gives me **room** to think about a family.
do: Keep improving my **writing** and saving steadily.
Look again at **teaching** in about five years.
feel: Fairly **calm**, with a small worry about the **paper**.
S4.quote: I'd still want children one day, and a computer taking newsroom jobs in ten years isn't a reason to put that off.
fieldNote: With ten years Vera puts **family hopes** ahead of career worry.
Her faith frames the future as **not fully hers** to control.
Her trigger is the Star **dropping print days** or Helen leaving.

steps.text: Stay on the Star's education and community beat
Use AI tools for council and school papers
Save a steady amount each month

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'd go from reporter to apprentice in a year, living in my old bedroom. What would help is proper paid apprenticeships for adults, not just for school leavers, and a bit of help with rent while you train.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the good news. Machines can write up the council meeting, but somebody has to notice the woman who's run the food bank for ten years without being thanked.

headlineQuote: Machines can write up the council meeting, but somebody has to notice the woman who's run the food bank for ten years without being thanked.
portrait: Vera is a **27-year-old** education and community reporter at a shrinking evening paper.
She's **single**, lives near her parents, sings in a church choir and lives on one wage.
She uses AI **now and then**, once colleagues have shown it works.
Her plans run from **teaching** in slower pictures to a **plumbing apprenticeship** in the fastest.
Her **faith and family** shape both her fears and her sense of what to do.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she'd have to start over as an apprentice within a year.
whatWouldHelp: Paid **adult apprenticeships** and help with **rent** while training.
